text: A default matplotlib chart is a fine first draft. Customizing is how you turn it into something you'd show a stakeholder. Almost everything is controlled through keyword arguments and methods on the axes.

Start with the line itself. Color, linewidth, linestyle and marker are all keyword arguments to plot. Give every series a label and it appears in the legend. And axhline draws a horizontal reference line across the chart, like a target. Colors matter here too: a colorblind-safe blue and a quiet grey dashed line keep the focus on the data.

Next, words and structure. Use annotate to point an arrow at the one moment that matters, here the September dip, so readers don't have to search for it. Format the axis with set major formatter, which turns raw tick values into dollars-and-k labels. Add light horizontal gridlines, remove the legend's frame, and hide the top and right spines.

Here's the result. The line is bold and colorblind-safe, the target is a dashed grey line, the title says revenue passed target in July, and an arrow labels the September dip. Every element is there because it helps the reader. Nothing is there just to look busy, and if you can't say why an element helps, delete it.

Finally, style. plt dot style dot available lists the built-in style sheets, and plt dot style dot use applies one to every chart made afterward. A style context applies it to just one chart. And rcParams sets defaults such as font size, so you write your preferences once instead of on every chart. The rule of thumb: customize to clarify, not to decorate.
Next up: seaborn for statistical plots.
